q: What does love mean in tennis?
a: Tennis uses a unique scoring system that can be confusing to newcomers. Points progress as 0 (called 'love'), 15, 30, 40, and game. If both players reach 40 (called 'deuce'), a player must win two consecutive points to win the game — the first point after deuce is 'advantage,' and if the same player wins the next point, they win the game. If the opponent wins the advantage point, it returns to deuce. A set is won by the first player to win six games with a two-game lead; if the set reaches 5-5, it extends to 7-5 or a tiebreak at 6-6 (in most tournaments). A match is typically best of three sets for women and best of five for men in Grand Slams. The origin of 'love' is believed to come from the French word 'l'oeuf' (egg), meaning zero.

q: What are the Grand Slam tennis tournaments?
Wimbledon, French Open, US Open, Australian Open explained
The four Grand Slams in tennis
Which are the most important tennis tournaments?
Grand Slam tennis history and differences
What makes Wimbledon different from other Slams?
a: The four Grand Slam tournaments are the most prestigious events in professional tennis. The Australian Open (January) is played on hard courts in Melbourne and is known for extreme heat conditions. The French Open (May-June) is played on red clay at Roland Garros in Paris, demanding exceptional stamina and sliding ability — Rafael Nadal holds a record 14 titles here. Wimbledon (June-July) is the oldest and most traditional Grand Slam, played on grass courts at the All England Club, with strict all-white dress code and no play on the middle Sunday. The US Open (August-September) is played on hard courts in New York and is known for its night-session atmosphere and the use of tiebreaks in final sets. Each tournament has unique traditions, surfaces, and playing conditions that test different aspects of a player's game.

q: What are the differences between clay, grass, and hard tennis courts?
Clay vs grass vs hard court tennis
How do different tennis surfaces affect gameplay?
Tennis surface characteristics and player preferences
a: Tennis surfaces dramatically affect the speed and style of play. Clay courts (red or green) are slow, producing high bounces and allowing players to slide into shots — they reward defensive skills, topspin, and stamina, and points are typically longer. Grass courts are the fastest surface, with low, skidding bounces and a slippery footing — they favor big servers and aggressive net players, and points are usually shorter. Hard courts (acrylic or asphalt) fall between clay and grass in speed, offering consistent bounces and suiting all-around players — they are the most common surface globally and used for the Australian and US Opens. The different surfaces have historically created specialist players who excel on one type, though modern champions like Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, and Novak Djokovic proved capable of winning on all surfaces.

q: Who are the greatest tennis players of all time?
Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic, Serena Williams explained
GOAT debate in tennis: Federer vs Nadal vs Djokovic
Greatest male and female tennis players
a: The tennis GOAT debate centers on the 'Big Three' of men's tennis. Roger Federer won 20 Grand Slams with elegant, all-court play and held the record for weeks at world No. 1. Rafael Nadal, the 'King of Clay,' holds 22 Grand Slams including a record 14 French Opens, known for his relentless topspin and fighting spirit. Novak Djokovic holds the record for most weeks at No. 1 and 24 Grand Slam titles (most by any man), excelling on all surfaces with unparalleled flexibility and return of serve. In women's tennis, Serena Williams won 23 Grand Slams (Open Era record), dominating with power and athleticism for over two decades. Other legends include Martina Navratilova (18 Slams), Steffi Graf (22 Slams including the 1988 Golden Slam), Chris Evert, Billie Jean King, Margaret Court (24 Slams), Rod Laver (two calendar-year Grand Slams), and Bjorn Borg.

q: What are the basic rules of tennis?
How does a tennis match work?
a: Tennis is played between two opponents (singles) or two teams of two (doubles) on a rectangular court divided by a net. The server must stand behind the baseline and hit the ball diagonally into the opponent's service box, with two attempts allowed per point (a fault on both attempts is a double fault, losing the point). Once the ball is in play, players hit the ball back and forth over the net, and a point ends when the ball bounces twice, a player fails to return it, or hits it out of bounds. In doubles, the court is wider (using the doubles sidelines) and teams alternate shots. Let serves (touching the net but landing in the correct box) are replayed. Matches are officiated by chair umpires and line judges, though electronic line calling is increasingly used at professional events.

q: How do points work in tennis rankings?
a: Professional tennis rankings are maintained by the ATP (men's) and WTA (women's) based on a 52-week rolling points system. Players earn points by performing well in tournaments, with Grand Slams awarding the most points (2000 for the winner), followed by Masters 1000 events, ATP 500 and 250 events (men), and WTA 1000, 500, and 250 events (women). A player's ranking is determined by their best results in the most recent 52 weeks, capped at a certain number of tournaments (19 for ATP, 16 for WTA). Rankings determine tournament seeding and entry eligibility. Novak Djokovic holds the record for the most weeks at world No. 1 in men's tennis, while Steffi Graf holds the women's record. The year-end No. 1 ranking is considered a significant achievement.
